Source: Shared care records (NHS England)
Relevance to Project: Core framing source on what NHS shared care records are across local geographies and care settings.
Key Point: Shared care records combine important, up-to-date information from multiple health and care organisations for direct care.
Security Issue: Secure cross-organisational access to current records.
Governance Issue: Local shared record governance across ICS/local partners.
Article Use: Use as the baseline NHS definition of shared care records.

Source: Shared care records – development and delivery (NHS England)
Relevance to Project: Directly useful for distinguishing shared care records from SCR and for deployment framing.
Key Point: Shared care records contain much more information than SCR and are sourced from multiple care organisations.
Governance Issue: Delivery model for local shared record implementation.
Article Use: Use to justify why near-complete records create different risk questions from SCR.

Source: Information Governance Framework: Shared Care Records (NHS Transformation Directorate)
Relevance to Project: Central governance source for lawful, secure operation of shared care records.
Key Point: Shared care records require explicit IG arrangements for safe and secure information sharing.
Security Issue: Information security controls for shared platforms.
Article Use: Use to anchor the governance architecture for cross-provider access.

Source: Information Governance Framework for Integrated Health and Care: Shared Care Records (NHS Transformation Directorate)
Relevance to Project: Detailed framework for controller relationships, rights, breach management and assurance.
Key Point: Shared care records move systems from separate records toward system-wide shared records.
Governance Issue: Joint controllers, assurance checklist, governance design.
Article Use: Use for your governance and accountability section.

Source: The Caldicott Principles (GOV.UK)
Relevance to Project: Foundational ethical-governance source for confidential patient information sharing.
Key Point: Confidential information should be used only when necessary, minimally, and with justified access, while duty to share can support better care.
Article Use: Use as the normative lens for evaluating complete-record access.

Source: National Data Guardian guidance on the appointment of Caldicott Guardians, their role and responsibilities (GOV.UK)
Relevance to Project: Important for accountability and oversight in multi-organisation record sharing.
Key Point: Caldicott Guardians are senior leads for the ethical and legal aspects of data sharing.
Security Issue: Oversight of inappropriate access and disclosure.
Article Use: Use to support recommendations on local accountability structures.

Source: Data saves lives: reshaping health and social care with data (GOV.UK)
Relevance to Project: Strategic context for connected data, trust and safe use across health and care.
Key Point: The strategy explicitly links better data use with the need to reassure the public that data will be handled safely and ethically.
Governance Issue: National strategic direction for data sharing.
Article Use: Use for policy context and public trust framing.

Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 / UK GDPR contents (Legislation.gov.uk)
Relevance to Project: Primary legal framework for personal data processing in the UK.
Key Point: UK GDPR sets core principles, lawful bases, accountability, and data subject rights.
Article Use: Use as the umbrella legal framework.

Source: UK GDPR Article 9 (Legislation.gov.uk)
Relevance to Project: Directly relevant because health data is special category data.
Key Point: Processing health data is prohibited unless an Article 9 condition applies.
Article Use: Use to explain why complete shared records need heightened justification.

Source: Data Protection Act 2018 contents (Legislation.gov.uk)
Relevance to Project: Supplements UK GDPR in UK law and is critical for health/social care processing conditions.
Key Point: DPA 2018 tailors UK GDPR and adds Schedule 1 conditions and safeguards.
Article Use: Use alongside UK GDPR for the legal analysis.

Source: Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 / special categories of personal data (Legislation.gov.uk)
Relevance to Project: Especially relevant for health and social care processing conditions.
Key Point: Schedule 1 includes conditions covering health care, social care and management of care systems/services.
Privacy Issue: Health data condition in domestic law.
Article Use: Use to tie direct care sharing to domestic legal conditions.

Source: Special category data (ICO) (Information Commissioner's Office)
Relevance to Project: Clear practical guidance on handling health data lawfully.
Key Point: Controllers need both an Article 6 lawful basis and a separate Article 9 condition.
Security Issue: Failure to structure lawful processing correctly.
Article Use: Use for practitioner-friendly legal interpretation.

Source: What are the conditions for processing? (ICO) (Information Commissioner's Office)
Relevance to Project: Important for identifying Article 9(2)(h) health/social care processing.
Key Point: Article 9(2)(h) supports necessary processing for provision or management of health and social care/services.
Privacy Issue: Lawful use of special category health data.
Article Use: Use to distinguish direct-care lawful processing from other bases.

Source: When is consent appropriate? (ICO) (Information Commissioner's Office)
Relevance to Project: Very useful for avoiding a common mistake in NHS data-sharing discussions.
Key Point: Implied consent for direct care confidentiality is not the same as GDPR consent as a lawful basis.
Security Issue: Misapplied consent models can weaken controls.
Governance Issue: Correct legal framing for direct-care sharing.
Article Use: Use to clarify legal misconceptions in Article 1.

Source: Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) (Information Commissioner's Office)
Relevance to Project: Essential source because cross-provider complete-record access is likely high-risk processing.
Key Point: DPIAs are a structured way to identify and mitigate data protection risks early.
Security Issue: Risk identification and mitigation before deployment.
Article Use: Use to argue DPIAs should be mandatory for shared-record expansions.

Source: What is a DPIA? (ICO) (Information Commissioner's Office)
Relevance to Project: Good concise explanation of DPIA purpose.
Key Point: A DPIA helps systematically analyse, identify and minimise data protection risks and demonstrate compliance.
Article Use: Use in the methods/governance argument of Article 1.

Source: Data protection by design and by default (ICO) (Information Commissioner's Office)
Relevance to Project: Highly relevant for architecture and system design of cross-provider records.
Key Point: Organisations must build technical and organisational measures into processing from the outset.
Article Use: Use to frame design recommendations for secure record sharing.

Source: GP Connect (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Core NHS service for cross-setting access to GP records.
Key Point: GP Connect allows authorised health and social care workers in multiple settings to access GP records.
Privacy Issue: Viewing GP-held patient information beyond registered practice.
Article Use: Use as a real-world example of cross-provider access already in operation.

Source: GP Connect: Access Record (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Directly aligned with your project’s focus on complete/near-complete record access.
Key Point: GP Connect Access Record makes patient medical information available to appropriate clinicians where needed for direct care.
Security Issue: Access management for clinicians away from registered practice.
Privacy Issue: Wider exposure of GP record content.
Governance Issue: Appropriateness of access and direct-care purpose.
Article Use: Use to discuss operational benefits and security/privacy trade-offs.

Source: GP Connect Access Record: HTML FHIR API (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Useful for technical architecture and what “read-only” access looks like.
Key Point: The API provides read-only viewing of a patient’s registered GP practice record inside EPR systems.
Security Issue: API security, read-only access, system integration.
Article Use: Use in the technical background section.

Source: GP Connect Access Record: Structured FHIR API (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Important for structured, machine-processable access rather than simple display.
Key Point: Structured coded data can be imported and processed by consuming systems via Spine.
Security Issue: Expanded attack surface through structured import.
Article Use: Use to distinguish display access from computable access.

Source: GP Connect transparency notice (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Important for legal transparency and public-facing accountability.
Key Point: Explains how patient data is accessed and shared through GP Connect for direct care.
Privacy Issue: Transparency about who accesses data and why.
Article Use: Use to evidence transparency obligations for cross-provider access.

Source: Summary Care Record (SCR) (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Essential comparator for your project because SCR is narrower than shared records/SPR.
Key Point: SCR is a national database of key patient information from GP records, especially medicines and allergies.
Security Issue: National service security and authorised access.
Privacy Issue: Limited summary rather than full record.
Article Use: Use as the “limited-record” comparator against fuller record models.

Source: Summary Care Records (SCR) – information for patients (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Useful for patient-facing understanding, opt-out, and trust.
Key Point: SCR is a short summary from GP records used by staff involved in care.
Article Use: Use when discussing patient trust and acceptable disclosure.

Source: Summary Care Record supplementary transparency notice (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Important for lawful processing and transparency in SCR use.
Key Point: Describes how NHS Digital, GPs and others may use SCR information in health and social care.
Security Issue: National access controls and use conditions.
Article Use: Use for legal/governance comparison with shared care records.

Source: Summary Care Record – HL7 V3 API (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Technical source for how SCR is accessed in systems.
Key Point: SCR can be accessed via API by authorised staff in direct care settings.
Security Issue: API access control and secure integration.
Privacy Issue: Summary data visibility outside GP setting.
Governance Issue: Technical route into national records service.
Article Use: Use for technical comparison with GP Connect.

Source: National Care Records Service (NCRS) (NHS England Digital)
Relevance to Project: Relevant because it signals the NHS direction for national patient information access.
Key Point: NCRS provides a quick, secure way for health and care workers to access national patient information.
Article Use: Use as an example of the NHS moving toward broader record access services.

Source: Interoperability (NHS England)
Relevance to Project: Strong source for standards-based information exchange.
Key Point: FHIR is the NHS’s key standard for passing healthcare data between systems; sensitive APIs require security patterns.
Security Issue: API security patterns and secure exchange.
Article Use: Use to connect record sharing with technical standards and controls.

Source: Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT) (dsptoolkit.nhs.uk)
Relevance to Project: Core organisational assurance mechanism across health and care.
Key Point: DSPT measures organisations against the National Data Guardian’s 10 data security standards.
Security Issue: Baseline cyber and information security maturity.
Article Use: Use as an operational governance control in Article 1.

Source: Digital clinical safety assurance (NHS England)
Relevance to Project: Important because safety risk and information risk meet in shared-record systems.
Key Point: DCB0129 is for manufacturers; DCB0160 is for deploying organisations.
Security Issue: Unsafe system behaviour causing patient harm.
Privacy Issue: Inappropriate data display/use can affect privacy and safety.
Article Use: Use to argue that record-access design is a safety issue as well as a privacy issue.

Source: DCB0129: Clinical Risk Management: its Application in the Manufacture of Health IT Systems (NHS Standards Directory)
Relevance to Project: Essential standard for suppliers building shared-record technologies.
Key Point: Manufacturers must evidence the clinical safety of health IT products.
Privacy Issue: Unsafe data presentation or omission affecting confidentiality or care.
Article Use: Use in any supplier/system-design discussion.

Source: DCB0160: Clinical Risk Management: its Application in the Deployment and Use of Health IT Systems (NHS Standards Directory)
Relevance to Project: Essential standard for NHS organisations deploying shared-record systems.
Key Point: Health and care organisations must assure the clinical safety of deployed health IT systems.
Privacy Issue: Privacy impacts from unsafe deployment choices.
Article Use: Use to show local NHS organisations cannot treat record access as only a vendor issue.

Source: Li E, Clarke J, Ashrafian H, Darzi A, Neves AL. The Impact of Electronic Health Record Interoperability on Safety and Quality of Care in High-Income Countries: Systematic Review (JMIR)
Relevance to Project: Directly relevant to the benefits side of your argument.
Key Point: Interoperability can improve safety and quality, but benefits depend on implementation and context.
Security Issue: Poor interoperability can create safety risks and incomplete information flows.
Article Use: Use to balance benefit claims against risk claims.

Source: Torab-Miandoab A, Samad-Soltani T, Jodati A, Rezaei-Hachesu P. Interoperability of heterogeneous health information systems: a systematic literature review (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Strong source on interoperability challenges and why records remain fragmented.
Key Point: Lack of interoperability reduces care quality and wastes resources.
Privacy Issue: Disjointed records can undermine appropriate access.
Governance Issue: Standards and governance needed for interoperability.
Article Use: Use to justify why shared records emerge as a policy response.

Source: Häyrinen K, Saranto K, Nykänen P. Definition, structure, content, use and impacts of electronic health records: a review of the research literature (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Still foundational for defining EHR scope and implications.
Key Point: EHRs are broader than isolated clinical notes and have structural, content and use implications.
Article Use: Use for definitional groundwork.

Source: Papoutsi C, Reed JE, Marston C, Lewis R, Majeed A, Bell D. Patient and public views about the security and privacy of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) in the UK (Springer)
Relevance to Project: One of the most directly relevant UK trust/privacy papers.
Key Point: Many respondents worried about the security of national EHRs and doubted the NHS could guarantee safety.
Privacy Issue: Public concern about misuse and breaches.
Article Use: Use in your patient trust section and UK context.

Source: Shen N, Bernier T, Sequeira L, et al. Understanding the patient privacy perspective on health information exchange: a systematic review (PubMed)
Relevance to Project: Excellent synthesis of what shapes patient attitudes to HIE.
Key Point: Patient privacy perspectives depend on trust, control, understanding, and perceived benefit.
Security Issue: Concerns about inappropriate sharing and breaches.
Privacy Issue: Perceived loss of privacy and control.
Article Use: Use to build the conceptual model of patient trust in Article 1.

Source: Esmaeilzadeh P, Sambasivan M. Patients’ support for health information exchange: a literature review and classification of key factors (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Good source on determinants of patient support for HIE.
Key Point: Patient support depends on privacy, security, trust, perceived usefulness and control.
Article Use: Use to translate trust into design/governance requirements.

Source: Busch-Casler J, Jalalzai M, Benis A, et al. Trust and Health Information Exchanges: Qualitative Analysis of the Intent to Share Personal Health Information (JMIR)
Relevance to Project: Useful for the trust and communication angle.
Key Point: Patients need to trust that HIE privacy policies and security measures are sufficient.
Privacy Issue: Privacy policy clarity and perceived risk.
Article Use: Use to support a trust-centred governance argument.

Source: Kisekka V, Giboney JS, Davis FD. The Effectiveness of Health Care Information Technologies: Evaluation of Trust, Security Beliefs, and Privacy as Determinants of Health Care Outcomes (PubMed)
Relevance to Project: Strong source linking privacy/security beliefs to behaviour and outcomes.
Key Point: Privacy concerns reduce positive attitudes toward HIE and record access, while trust improves perceived care quality.
Security Issue: Security belief affects adoption and use.
Privacy Issue: Privacy concern affects willingness to use/access.
Article Use: Use to connect governance quality with user and patient outcomes.

Source: de Carvalho Junior MA, Bandiera-Paiva P, et al. Health Information System Role-Based Access Control Current Security Trends and Challenges (PubMed)
Relevance to Project: Directly relevant to role-based access across multiple provider settings.
Key Point: RBAC remains central in health information systems but has limitations and implementation challenges.
Security Issue: Over-privileged or poorly designed role access.
Governance Issue: Need for careful role engineering and review.
Article Use: Use to frame RBAC as necessary but insufficient for complete-record access.

Source: Dimitropoulos L, Rizk S. A state-based approach to privacy and security for interoperable health information exchange (PubMed)
Relevance to Project: Still highly relevant for HIE governance design.
Key Point: Interoperable exchange needs coordinated privacy and security controls, not just technical connectivity.
Article Use: Use for conceptualising governance across providers.

Source: Fernández-Alemán JL, Señor IC, Lozoya PÁO, Toval A. Security and privacy in electronic health records: a systematic literature review (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Classic review on EHR security/privacy requirements.
Key Point: EHR systems must reconcile privacy protection with availability and usability.
Article Use: Use as a foundational literature review.

Source: Tertulino R, Antunes N, Morais H. Privacy in electronic health records: a systematic mapping study (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Strong recent overview of EHR privacy research gaps.
Key Point: Major challenge is protecting privacy without undermining performance and interoperability.
Article Use: Use for the contemporary literature gap section.

Source: Kruse CS, Smith B, Vanderlinden H, Nealand A. Security Techniques for the Electronic Health Records (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Helpful review of practical security controls in EHR environments.
Key Point: Privacy and security are major barriers to EHR adoption, and layered security techniques are needed.
Security Issue: Authentication, encryption, audit and access control.
Article Use: Use to summarise common control families.

Source: Menon AK, Jiang X, Kim J, et al. Detecting Inappropriate Access to Electronic Health Records Using Collaborative Filtering (PMC)
Relevance to Project: Excellent insider-threat and auditability source.
Key Point: Many EHR environments rely on broad access plus ex post audit; machine methods can improve detection of inappropriate access.
Article Use: Use for the insider threat and auditability section.

Source: Chen Y, Nyemba S, Malin B. Auditing Medical Records Accesses via Healthcare Interaction Networks (PMC)
Relevance to Project: Strong source on audit logs and detection logic.
Key Point: Auditing authenticated insiders is critical for detecting inappropriate medical-record access.
Security Issue: Insider threat detection through audit trails.
Article Use: Use to support recommendations on access-log review.

Source: Hedda M, Bellika JG, Hartvigsen G. Evaluating the Effectiveness of Auditing Rules for Electronic Health Records (PMC)
Relevance to Project: Useful for showing that not all audit rules are equally effective.
Key Point: High-risk auditing rules can be evaluated and ranked by potential risk.
Privacy Issue: Delayed or missed privacy breach detection.
Article Use: Use to argue for smarter, risk-based audit controls.

Source: Rule A, Chiang MF, Hribar MR. Using electronic health record audit logs to study clinical activity (PMC)
Relevance to Project: Good methodological source on what audit logs can and cannot reveal.
Key Point: Audit logs are valuable but require careful interpretation and standardisation.
Governance Issue: Audit data governance and analytic maturity.
Article Use: Use to temper claims about auditability.

Source: Tierney WM, Alpert SA, Byrket A, et al. Provider responses to patients controlling access to their electronic health records: a prospective cohort study in primary care (PubMed)
Relevance to Project: One of the most useful empirical sources on break-glass behaviour.
Key Point: Providers used “break the glass” access when data redactions obstructed care.
Article Use: Use to discuss break-glass access as necessary but governance-heavy.

Source: de Oliveira MT, Carrasco RA, et al. A break-glass protocol based on ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption to access medical records in the cloud (Springer)
Relevance to Project: Strong technical source on controlled emergency access.
Key Point: Break-glass can be engineered with cryptographic controls so emergency teams access only relevant data.
Article Use: Use for a future-design recommendation section.
